Ceremonial Law
ser-uh-MOH-nee-uhl LAW
noun (theology)
From ceremonial (Latin caerimonia, a sacred rite) + law; the ritual ordinances of Moses — sacrifices, priesthood, feasts, purities — fulfilled in Christ.

Biblical Definition

The ceremonial law is that part of the law given through Moses which concerned the worship and ritual life of Israel: the sacrifices and offerings, the priesthood and tabernacle, the feasts and sabbaths, the clean and unclean, circumcision and the purities. The Reformed tradition has long distinguished, within the one law of God, three uses or kinds: the moral law (the Ten Commandments, the abiding rule of righteousness), the judicial or civil law (the ordering of Israel as a nation, whose general equity continues), and the ceremonial law (the shadows of things to come). The ceremonial law was never an end in itself; it was a great preaching of the gospel in type and shadow, pointing forward to Christ. Every lamb slain, every priest interceding, every feast kept, was a finger pointing to Him who is the true Lamb, the true Priest, the true Passover. Therefore, when Christ came and fulfilled them, the ceremonies passed away: the veil was torn, the sacrifices ceased, the wall between Jew and Gentile fell. "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday... which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ" (Col 2:16–17). This dictionary confesses that the ceremonial law was holy and good, fully fulfilled and abrogated in Christ, and now read not for ritual obligation but for the gospel it everywhere preaches.

Webster 1828 Definition

The ritual part of the Mosaic law — sacrifices, priesthood, feasts, purities — distinguished from the abiding moral law and the judicial law. A great preaching of the gospel in type and shadow, pointing to Christ, and fulfilled and abrogated in Him (Col 2:16–17).

CEREMONIAL LAW, noun. The ritual ordinances of the Mosaic law — sacrifices, priesthood, feasts, and purities.

Distinguished in the Reformed tradition from the moral law and the judicial (civil) law.

Never an end in itself, but a preaching of the gospel in type and shadow.

Every sacrifice and feast pointed forward to Christ — the true Lamb, Priest, and Passover.

Fulfilled and abrogated in Christ; the shadow gives way to the body (Col 2:16–17).

Key Scripture

Col 2:17 — "Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ."

Heb 10:1 — "For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect."

Heb 9:12 — "Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us."

Matt 5:17 — "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."

Modern Corruption

The ceremonial law is corrupted by two opposite errors: a Judaizing that would bind its shadows on the Christian conscience again — sabbaths, feasts, food laws — as though Christ had not fulfilled them, and a careless dispensationalism or antinomianism that, in casting off the ceremonies, throws out the abiding moral law along with them.

expand to see more

The first corruption is to re-impose the shadows. Whether in the old Judaizers who troubled Galatia, or in modern movements that bind festival-keeping, food laws, or ceremonial sabbaths upon believers, the error is the same: to go back to the shadow when the body has come. Paul forbids it — let no man judge you in meat, drink, or holy day, which are a shadow; the body is of Christ (Col 2:16–17). To cling to the type is to deny that the Lamb has come.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but the opposite corruption confuses the kinds of law. Some, rightly seeing the ceremonial law abrogated, sweep away the moral law with it, as though the Ten Commandments too were shadows that passed at the cross. They were not. Christ came not to destroy but to fulfil (Matt 5:17); the ceremonial law is fulfilled and gone, but the moral law abides as the rule of the redeemed life. The principle to recover is the careful distinction: the shadows are fulfilled in Christ and read now for the gospel they preach, while the moral law stands.

Hebrew Roots

From Latin caerimonia (a sacred rite) + law; the ritual ordinances of Moses — shadows of Christ — fulfilled and abrogated in Him.

expand to see more

Latin caerimonia, a sacred rite or ceremony

The ritual part of the Mosaic law: sacrifice, priesthood, feast, purity

One of three kinds: moral, judicial, and ceremonial

A shadow of good things to come (Heb 10:1)

Fulfilled and abrogated in Christ; the body is His (Col 2:17)

Usage

"The ceremonial law preached the gospel in shadow until the body, Christ, appeared."

"When Christ fulfilled the ceremonial law, the sacrifices ceased and the veil was torn."

"The ceremonial law is abrogated, but the moral law abides as the rule of life."
